title: Leading Effective Meetings
grammar: Present Perfect vs Past Simple in updates
objective: Chair a professional meeting, manage time and keep people focused.
grammarDetail: Present Perfect vs Past Simple in updates.  We have finished the proposal (result matters now) vs We finished the proposal last Friday (focus on when). Both are common in meetings.
grammarDeepDive:
In meetings, you constantly report what has happened and what was done. English gives you two tenses that both talk about the past, but with different focus:

 Present Perfect (have/has + past participle) — the result matters now . We don't say when exactly: 'We have finished the proposal — we can move forward.' The listener thinks: 'Great, it's done, what's next?'

 Past Simple (verb + -ed / irregular) — we state when it happened: 'We finished the proposal last Friday.' The listener thinks: 'OK, Friday, noted.'

Key signals:
- already, just, yet, this week, so far → Present Perfect
- yesterday, last Monday, two hours ago, in March → Past Simple

title: Writing Effective Business Emails
objective: Write clear, professional emails with structure, tone and appropriate formality.
grammarDetail: Passive voice. Useful for a more formal or neutral tone: The report has been updated. Your request will be reviewed by Friday. Use actively but don't overdo it.
grammarDeepDive:
The passive voice switches the focus from who did the action to what was done . This is very useful in professional emails because it sounds neutral, polite and objective.

 Active : We have updated the report. (focus on 'we')
 Passive : The report has been updated. (focus on 'the report')

The structure is: subject + be (in the right tense) + past participle .

Common tenses in business emails:
- Present Simple passive: 'Invoices are sent on the first of each month.' 
- Present Perfect passive: 'The report has been updated.' 
- Future passive: 'Your request will be reviewed by Friday.' 
- Present Continuous passive: 'Your order is being processed.'

title: Mastering Calls and Video Meetings
objective: Handle phone and video calls professionally, including turn-taking in larger meetings.
grammarDetail: Interrupting politely. Useful phrases: Sorry to jump in, If I may, Can I add something quickly, Just a quick point on that.
grammarDeepDive:
Interrupting is not rude in English — it is necessary, especially on calls with many people. What matters is how you interrupt. English has a clear set of softening phrases that signal 'I want to speak' without cutting someone off.

 To enter a conversation: 
- 'Sorry to jump in — ...' (most common, friendly)
- 'If I may, ...' (slightly more formal)
- 'Can I add something quickly?' (asks permission)
- 'Just a quick point on that.' (short, direct)

 To hand the turn to someone else: 
- 'Over to you, Harry.' 
- 'I think Sophie wanted to say something.' 
- 'Shall we hear from the Brazil desk?'

title: Delivering Business Presentations
grammar: Linking and contrast — however, on the other hand
objective: Structure and deliver a persuasive business presentation at intermediate level.
grammarDetail: Linkers of contrast. Use however, on the other hand, nevertheless, that said to move between arguments smoothly. Example: The market is tough; however, our position has strengthened.
grammarDeepDive:
In presentations, you often need to move from one argument to a contrasting one. English uses special linking words for this. They make your speaking and writing sound structured and professional.

 however — the most common formal contrast word. It replaces 'but' in a more polished way: 'The market is tough; however, our position is strong.' 
 on the other hand — used to present a second, contrasting perspective: 'Raw sugar is more profitable. On the other hand, refined sugar offers long-term stability.'

title: Negotiation: Finding the Win-Win
objective: Negotiate professionally using structured conditionals and value-trading phrases.
grammarDetail: Conditionals for negotiation. Use If you can… we could… or We would be able to… if you… . Example: If you can commit to a two-year contract, we could offer a better rate.
grammarDeepDive:
Conditionals are the grammar of negotiation. They let you propose a trade without committing to it: 'If you can commit to a two-year contract, we could offer a better rate.' The if-clause sets the condition; the main clause shows the reward. This structure keeps both sides flexible.

At Rise level, we use two conditional patterns:

 Type 1 (realistic offers) : if + present simple, will/can/could + base verb.
 'If you increase the volume, we can reduce the price.' 
This sounds confident and practical — the deal is realistic.

title: Making Better Decisions
grammar: Modals of possibility — might, could, may
objective: Discuss decisions, weigh options and express uncertainty professionally.
grammarDetail: Modals of possibility. Use might, could, may to talk about possible outcomes without overclaiming. Example: This might work in the short term. That could be risky.
grammarDeepDive:
When we talk about future outcomes, risks or options at work, we rarely say things with 100% certainty. English has three modal verbs that let you express possibility without overclaiming:

 might — something is possible but not certain: 'Freight costs might rise next quarter.' 
 could — something is possible, often with a condition: 'This could work if we adjust the timeline.' 
 may — similar to 'might', slightly more formal: 'The client may prefer a shorter contract.' 

All three are followed by the base verb (no 'to', no '-s'): 'It might work. She could help. They may agree.' 

Negatives: might not, could not (couldn't), may not. Note: 'may not' does not contract to 'mayn't' in modern Eng

title: Problem Solving in Practice
objective: Diagnose business problems systematically and explain root causes.
grammarDetail: Reason connectors.  Because (informal), due to / owing to (formal, followed by a noun), since (when the reason is already known). Example: The delay was due to a missing approval. Since we know the cause, we can act.
grammarDeepDive:
When explaining problems and root causes, you need to connect a result with a reason . English offers three main connectors, each with a slightly different use:

 because + clause (subject + verb): the most common and versatile.
 'The report was late because the data file was not shared on time.' 

 due to / owing to + noun phrase : more formal, common in written reports.
 'The delay was due to a missing approval.' 
Note: due to is often interchangeable with owing to , though due to is more common in modern business English.

 since + clause : used when the reason is already known by both speakers.
 'Since we know the root cause, we can now plan the fix.'

title: Project Management Fundamentals
objective: Plan, track and report on a project using professional project-management language.
grammarDetail: Future continuous and future perfect.  By Friday, we will be testing the prototype. By the end of the month, we will have delivered two out of three milestones. Common in PM status reports.
grammarDeepDive:
In project management, you often need to describe what will be happening at a future point or what will be completed by a deadline. English gives you two precise tenses for this:

 Future continuous (will be + -ing) — an action in progress at a future point:
 'Next week, we will be running user tests every day.' 
 'At 3 pm tomorrow, I will be meeting the sponsor.' 

 Future perfect (will have + past participle) — an action completed before a future point:
 'By the end of Q2, we will have delivered three milestones.' 
 'By Friday, the team will have finalised the design.' 

Key time markers:
- Future continuous: this time next week, at 3 pm, next Monday, during Q3 
- Future perfect: by Friday

title: Productivity and Focused Work
objective: Discuss productivity habits, focus and the economics of deep work.
grammarDetail: Gerunds after prepositions. Example: She is good at focusing. I am tired of being interrupted. He is interested in improving his productivity.
grammarDeepDive: In English, when a verb comes immediately after a preposition, it must take the -ing form (the gerund). This rule has no exceptions. We say 'good at focusing' , 'tired of waiting' , 'interested in learning' . The preposition demands a noun or a noun-like form — and the gerund is the verb acting as a noun. This is one of the most common grammar patterns in professional English. In meetings, emails and reports, we constantly use phrases like 'instead of sending' , 'before starting' , 'after finishing' , 'responsible for managing' . title: Networking with Confidence
objective: Navigate professional networking events with confidence and natural conversation.
grammarDetail: Question tags. Common in British small talk: It's a great venue, isn't it? You've worked in commodities for a while, haven't you? They invite the other person to respond.
grammarDeepDive: Question tags are short questions added to the end of a statement. They are extremely common in British English, especially in small talk, networking and informal professional conversation. The pattern is simple: if the main clause is positive, the tag is negative; if the main clause is negative, the tag is positive. For example: 'You work in sugar, don't you ?' and 'You don't work in freight, do you ?'  The tag always uses the same auxiliary verb as the main clause. If the main clause uses is , the tag uses isn't . If it uses have (as a perfect auxiliary), the tag uses haven't . If there is no auxiliary, we use do/does/did . title: The Art of Useful Feedback
objective: Give and receive feedback with clarity, kindness and specificity.
grammarDetail: Reported speech. Useful when summarising feedback from others: The client said they found the proposal too technical. My manager told me she would like a shorter version.
grammarDeepDive: Reported speech (also called indirect speech) is how we tell someone what another person said, without quoting their exact words. In professional English, we use it constantly — in meetings, emails, and feedback conversations. Instead of saying 'The client said: "The proposal is too long"' , we say 'The client said the proposal was too long' . The meaning is the same, but reported speech sounds more professional and is easier to weave into discussion. The main rule is the tense shift : when the reporting verb (said, told, mentioned, explained) is in the past, the tenses inside the reported clause shift back one step. title: Status Reports and Escalation
objective: Write structured status reports and escalate issues professionally.
grammarDetail: Reporting verbs. Build a small bank: to confirm, to highlight, to flag, to note, to raise, to escalate. Example: I'd like to flag a risk on the delivery side. I can confirm the milestone has been met.
grammarDeepDive: Reporting verbs are the tools you use to present information in a professional, structured way. Instead of saying 'I want to tell you something', you say 'I'd like to flag a risk' or 'I can confirm the result'. Each verb carries a slightly different meaning and sets the reader's expectations before they even finish the sentence. The most common reporting verbs in business are confirm (yes, it happened), highlight (look at this — it matters), flag (warning — there is a risk), note (for the record), raise (bring up for discussion), and escalate (pass upward because it needs a bigger decision). title: Business Writing That Gets Read
objective: Write business documents that respect the reader's time and effort.
grammarDetail: Cutting fillers. Remove phrases like in order to (to), at this moment in time (now), it should be noted that (—), the fact that (that). Your sentences will land harder.
grammarDeepDive: In business English, shorter is almost always better. Readers are busy. They skim emails, reports and memos looking for the key point. If your message is buried under filler phrases, half your audience will never find it. Concise writing means removing words that add no meaning. The most common fillers in business writing are: in order to (just use 'to'), at this moment in time (just use 'now'), it should be noted that (delete it entirely), due to the fact that (use 'because'), and we are writing to inform you that (just say the thing). title: Leading Difficult Conversations
objective: Run a difficult conversation at work with calm, structure and outcome focus.
grammarDetail: Softeners and reformulation. Phrases like I'd like to share something that has been on my mind, I may have misread this, but, I wonder whether, let me put it differently.
grammarDeepDive: Softeners are phrases that make a difficult message easier to hear without removing the message itself. In English, we use them constantly in professional life: I may have misread this, but… , I wonder whether… , I'd like to share something… . They signal to the listener that you are being thoughtful, not attacking. The message still lands — it just arrives more gently. Reformulation is the skill of saying the same thing in a different way when the first attempt did not land well. Phrases like let me put that differently , what I mean is , and to be clearer allow you to correct course mid-conversation without losing face. title: Managing Up and Managing Stakeholders
objective: Influence without authority — manage senior stakeholders with structured communication.
grammarDetail: Type 2 Conditional for diplomacy.  If I were in your position, I would… / If we had a little more time, we could… Softens suggestions to senior audiences.
grammarDeepDive: In business English, being right is not always enough — you also need to sound respectful. The Conditional Type 2 (also called the Second Conditional) is one of the best tools for making suggestions to senior people without sounding pushy. Instead of saying 'You should do this' , you say 'If I were in your position, I would do this' . The meaning is the same, but the tone is completely different. The structure is: If + past simple, would + base verb . The past tense does not refer to the past — it creates distance and politeness. title: Working Across Cultures
grammar: Advanced comparatives — far more, significantly less
objective: Navigate cultural differences in international business with nuance.
grammarDetail: Advanced comparatives. Use far more, significantly less, considerably better, noticeably different to make comparisons more precise.
grammarDeepDive: In everyday English, we compare things with simple words like more and less . But in business English, especially when discussing cultures, markets and strategies, we need to be more precise . Instead of saying 'Japanese meetings are more formal' , we can say 'Japanese meetings are significantly more formal' . The meaning is sharper, and the speaker sounds more confident and knowledgeable. The main intensifiers are: far, significantly, considerably, noticeably, substantially, slightly, marginally . title: Data Storytelling
grammar: Describing trends — rose / fell / remained stable
objective: Turn data into clear, memorable business stories and charts.
grammarDetail: Trend verbs.  Rose, fell, climbed, dropped, remained stable, plateaued, peaked, recovered. Example: Sales rose sharply in Q1, plateaued in Q2, and recovered in Q3.
grammarDeepDive: When we present data in English, we use a specific set of trend verbs to describe what happened. The most important ones are: rose, fell, climbed, dropped, remained stable, plateaued, peaked, recovered, fluctuated . These verbs are intransitive — the subject does the action by itself. We say 'Sales rose' , not 'Sales were risen' . The price rises; we do not rise the price (we raise it). To make descriptions more precise, we add adverbs that describe the speed or size of the change: sharply, steadily, gradually, slightly, dramatically, significantly . title: Leading Through Change
objective: Lead a team through organisational change with clear communication and empathy.
grammarDetail: Sequencers and discourse markers.  To start with, in the first place, on top of that, more importantly, in particular, finally. Structure long explanations into logical steps.
grammarDeepDive: Sequencers and discourse markers are words and phrases that help you organise what you say into a logical order. In business English, they are essential when you need to explain a plan, walk someone through a process, or deliver a message that has several parts. Without them, even a good message sounds like a random collection of ideas. The most common sequencers are to start with, first of all, in the first place, secondly, on top of that, more importantly, in particular, furthermore, finally, and to sum up . Each one tells the listener where they are in the message: at the beginning, in the middle, or near the end. Think of them as road signs that keep the audience from getting lost. Both

title: Building Long-Term Client Relationships
objective: Nurture client relationships beyond transactions, in line with Czarnikow's tradition.
grammarDetail: Present Perfect for long relationships.  We have been working together for eight years. I have known him since he joined the industry. Essential for talking about history that still matters today.
grammarDeepDive: The Present Perfect is the tense you need when you want to talk about something that started in the past and is still true now . In business, this happens all the time: relationships that are still active, partnerships that are still running, clients you still work with. Whenever the past connects to the present, Present Perfect is the right choice. The structure is straightforward: have / has + past participle . We use for to say how long something has lasted ( for eight years ) and since to say when it started ( since 2016 ). Both answer the question 'how long?', but from different angles. title: Ethics, Compliance and Integrity
grammar: Modal verbs of obligation — must, shall, be expected to
objective: Discuss professional ethics and compliance with appropriate formal register.
grammarDetail: Modal verbs of obligation.  Must for strict rules, shall for formal / legal language, are expected to for professional norms. Example: Employees must disclose any conflict of interest. Managers are expected to lead by example.
grammarDeepDive: In business English, we use modal verbs of obligation to talk about rules, duties and professional expectations. The three most important ones are must , shall , and be expected to . Each one carries a different weight, and choosing the right one tells the listener how serious the obligation is.  Must is the strongest. It means 'this is a firm rule — you have no choice'. We use it for policies, legal requirements, and zero-tolerance rules: Employees must disclose conflicts of interest.  Shall appears in formal and legal documents — contracts, codes of conduct, compliance policies. It means roughly the same as 'must', but it sounds more official: The report shall be filed within seven days.
